summary: Earth drawn from real maps: every splat sits at its place's measured height and has its place's measured color, and each named feature is where the planetary gazetteer puts it. The relief, the turning speed and the lighting are simplified, and each simplification is labeled in the toy.

claims.claim: Earth turns once every 23.9345 hours (its sidereal day), sped up by the chosen factor.
claims.how: Each frame the drive adds the elapsed time times the speed-up, over the day's length, to the turn.

simplified: The relief is exaggerated by default (ten or twenty times; Pluto, Ceres and Vesta are drawn at true height), as chosen and labeled in the Toy tab; close up during a fly it eases to at most twice its height. True height is one choice away.
The world turns thousands of times faster than real (labeled in the Toy tab: an hour or a day each second).
North is always up and the sun stays near the equator's plane: the axial tilt and the seasons are left out.
The sun shades each slope by the cosine of its angle to the sun (Lambert's law) and leaves the night side dark, but nothing casts a shadow, and real surfaces scatter light in more complicated ways.
The global map has about 1,000 by 500 heights and 2,000 by 1,000 colors; only the patches round the named features are sharper.
The oceans are drawn flat at sea level; there are no clouds; the blue rim of air is a drawn glow.
The city lights are NASA's 2016 composite of cloud-free nights, not one night.
